## Start here {#start}

This guide shows how to choose the assumptions, read the results, and use the
main options of **CohortHonestDiD `r as.character(packageVersion("CohortHonestDiD"))`**,
which implements Liu (2026), *Cohort-Anchored HonestDiD*. For a shorter
introduction, see `vignette("getting-started", package = "CohortHonestDiD")`.
For an applied analysis, read [estimation](#fit), [targets](#targets), and
[reading results](#results). For estimates from other software, see
[external estimates](#external); [numerical controls](#controls) explains
computing costs and unresolved searches.

Write \(g\) for a cohort's adoption index on the ordered analysis grid, \(t\)
for a period index, and \(s=t-g+1\). Period \(s=1\) is the adoption period and
\(s=0\) the last untreated period. Calendar labels are kept for display, but
the restrictions use the ordered grid.

A cohort's block bias \(\Delta_{g,s}\) is its untreated-outcome trend relative
to its initial control group, the units still untreated when it adopts, under
the estimator's normalization. It enters the bias of the estimated
coefficients through a known bias map, \(\delta=W\Delta\). The sensitivity
restrictions apply to block biases; they place no restriction on how treatment
effects change over time. The guide uses these terms:

- **Procedures.** The conditional procedure (Conditional) and the conditional
  least-favorable hybrid (C-LF) of Andrews, Roth, and Pakes (2023) invert
  tests, so a confidence set can consist of several pieces. The fixed-length
  confidence interval (FLCI) of Armstrong and Kolesár (2018) is an optimized
  linear estimate plus or minus a half-length; it is available only under SD.
- **SD scope.** The post-only restriction (`full.path = FALSE`) bounds the
  slope changes that involve post-treatment periods. The full-path restriction
  (`full.path = TRUE`) also bounds those among pre-treatment periods.
- **Plug-in identified set.** The identified set computed as if the estimated
  coefficients were the true ones. ATT plots show it as a shaded band.
- **Framework.** Cohort inference (`framework = "cohort"`, the default)
  restricts each cohort's block bias. Aggregate inference restricts the
  aggregated event-study coefficients instead. Both support ATT and dynamic
  targets; cohort-dynamic targets require the cohort framework.

| Restriction | Meaning of the bound | Procedures | Default procedure | Default SD scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Second differences (SD) | Change in the slope of a cohort's block-bias path between consecutive periods; outcome units | FLCI, Conditional, C-LF | C-LF | Post-only (full path for FLCI) |
| Relative magnitudes (RM) | Post-treatment change relative to the cohort's largest pre-treatment change; no units | Conditional, C-LF | C-LF | Not applicable |

The paper recommends cohort inference with the Conditional or C-LF procedure,
under the post-only restriction for SD; the defaults are cohort inference with
C-LF, post-only under SD. `cohort_fit(covariance = "CR2")` gives
the bias-reduced covariance ([Section 2](#cr2)). Every interval in this guide
is pointwise, not a simultaneous band over periods or bounds.

The sensitivity approach is that of Rambachan and Roth (2023), *A More Credible
Approach to Parallel Trends*, Review of Economic Studies, 90(5), 2555–2591,
<https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdad018>. The data are the county minimum-wage application
of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021), *Difference-in-Differences with Multiple
Time Periods*, Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 200–230.

The code below uses three small helpers to print tables.

```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4.8, dpi = 120, warning = TRUE, message = TRUE)
library(CohortHonestDiD)
library(ggplot2)
tab <- function(x, digits = 5, ...) knitr::kable(x, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, ...)
sets <- function(x) x$intervals[, c("target", "M", "component", "lower", "upper", "success", "status")]
rows <- function(xs, labels = names(xs)) do.call(rbind, Map(function(x, label) {
  cbind(example = label, sets(x))
}, xs, labels))
```

## 1. Fit the minimum-wage application {#fit}

The bundled outcome `Y` is log teen employment. `D` equals one from the first
year in which a county's state minimum wage exceeds the federal minimum of
\$5.15, and treatment is absorbing.

```{r application-data}
data(minimum_wage)
tab(data.frame(rows = nrow(minimum_wage),
  counties = length(unique(minimum_wage$id)),
  first_year = min(minimum_wage$year), last_year = max(minimum_wage$year),
  periods = length(unique(minimum_wage$year))))
tab(head(minimum_wage[c("id", "year", "Y", "D")]))
```

### Formula, column names, and estimator choice

The formula must be exactly `outcome ~ treatment`, with the unit and time
columns in `index`, in that order. Covariates and transformations are not
supported.

```{r empirical-fits}
fit_imp <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                      estimator = "imp")
fit_nyt <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                      estimator = "cs_nyt")
fit_nt <- cohort_fit(data = minimum_wage, Y = "Y", D = "D", index = c("id", "year"),
                     estimator = "cs_nt")
print(fit_imp)
```

`imp` is the imputation estimator; `cs_nyt` and `cs_nt` are the
Callaway-Sant'Anna estimators with not-yet-treated and never-treated controls.
The column-name interface used for `fit_nt` is equivalent to the formula;
supply one or the other.

```{r estimator-comparison}
empirical <- list(imp = fit_imp, cs_nyt = fit_nyt, cs_nt = fit_nt)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(empirical), function(nm) {
  x <- empirical[[nm]]
  j <- x$coordinate_info$type == "post"
  data.frame(estimator = nm, cohort = x$coordinate_info$cohort[j],
    relative_period = x$coordinate_info$relative_period[j],
    estimate = as.numeric(coef(x)[j]), se = sqrt(diag(vcov(x)))[j])
}))
tab(comparison)
```

The rows compare the same cohort-period cells; the estimators differ because
they use different comparisons, in their control units and baseline periods.
The full covariance includes dependence across periods and across cohorts.

### Support and covariance diagnostics

```{r empirical-diagnostics}
tab(fit_imp$diagnostics$cohort_counts)
tab(data.frame(estimator = names(empirical),
  covariance_rank = vapply(empirical, function(x) x$diagnostics$covariance_rank, numeric(1)),
  normalized_dimension = vapply(empirical, function(x) x$diagnostics$normalized_dimension, numeric(1))))
plot(fit_imp, type = "dynamic", main = "Minimum wage: conventional event study",
     xlab = "Relative period (1 = adoption)", ylab = "Log teen employment")
```

The coefficient normalizations reduce the covariance rank by design, so compare
the rank with `normalized_dimension`, and check the cluster and cell counts.
With very few clusters, the estimated covariance can be unreliable even when
the computation succeeds. `plot(fit)` shows conventional 95% pointwise
intervals.

## 2. Weights, clusters, and panel histories {#histories}

By default, the unit identifier defines the clusters and every unit has weight
one. `cluster` and `weights` each accept a column name or a row-aligned vector.
Both must be fixed within unit, so a time-varying population series cannot
serve as weights; weights must also be positive and finite.

### State clustering and fixed baseline weights

For illustration, the next fits cluster by state and weight each county by its
baseline employment level. The rest of the guide is unweighted.

```{r empirical-weights-clusters}
baseline <- minimum_wage[minimum_wage$year == min(minimum_wage$year), c("id", "Y")]
baseline$fixed_weight <- exp(baseline$Y) / mean(exp(baseline$Y))
weighted_data <- minimum_wage
weighted_data$fixed_weight <- baseline$fixed_weight[match(weighted_data$id, baseline$id)]
fit_state <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                        estimator = "cs_nt", cluster = "state")
fit_weighted <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = weighted_data, index = c("id", "year"),
                           estimator = "cs_nt", cluster = "state",
                           weights = "fixed_weight")
tab(data.frame(fit = c("unit clusters", "state clusters", "state clusters, fixed weights"),
  clusters = c(fit_nt$diagnostics$n_clusters, fit_state$diagnostics$n_clusters,
               fit_weighted$diagnostics$n_clusters)))
conventional_att <- function(x) {
  post <- x$coordinate_info$type == "post"
  w <- numeric(length(coef(x)))
  w[post] <- x$cohort_masses[as.character(x$coordinate_info$cohort[post])]
  w <- w / sum(w)
  c(estimate = sum(w * coef(x)), se = sqrt(drop(t(w) %*% vcov(x) %*% w)))
}
weighted_comparison <- t(vapply(list(unit_clusters = fit_nt,
  state_clusters = fit_state, state_clusters_fixed_weights = fit_weighted),
  conventional_att, c(estimate = 0, se = 0)))
tab(data.frame(fit = rownames(weighted_comparison), weighted_comparison))
```

Changing the clusters changes the estimated uncertainty; changing the weights
can also change the estimand and the estimates. The default covariance,
`covariance = "CR1"`, sums centered cohort-period scores within clusters and
multiplies the sum of their outer products by \(G/(G-1)\cdot(n-1)/(n-p)\), for
\(G\) clusters, \(n\) usable rows, and \(p\) nonempty cohort-period cells. The
paper's minimum-wage results use county clusters, as in the original study.
Because minimum wages change at the state level, the paper's appendix also
reports state-clustered results without the 2004 cohort, which lies in a single
state.

### The bias-reduced CR2 covariance {#cr2}

`covariance = "CR2"` replaces the CR1 multiplier with the bias-reduced
adjustment of Bell and McCaffrey (2002): each cluster's score is divided by
\(\sqrt{1-p_c}\), where \(p_c\) is the cluster's share of the units of its
cohort, measured by the unit weights when `weights` is supplied. Never-treated
units form their own group. If a cluster contains units of several cohorts,
the part of its score from each cohort is divided by \(\sqrt{1-p}\), with \(p\)
its share of that cohort.
The paper recommends CR2 with Conditional or C-LF inference when some cohorts
contain only a few units or clusters. On unbalanced panels, CR2, like the bias
map, is an approximation; `?cohort_fit` gives the details.

```{r cr2-covariance}
fit_state_cr2 <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = minimum_wage, index = c("id", "year"),
                            estimator = "cs_nt", cluster = "state", covariance = "CR2")
print(fit_state_cr2)
shares <- fit_state_cr2$cluster_shares
tab(do.call(rbind, lapply(split(shares, shares$cohort), function(z)
  data.frame(cohort = z$cohort[1], clusters = nrow(z),
    largest_share = max(z$share), whole_cohort_clusters = sum(z$factor == 0)))))
tab(data.frame(covariance = c("CR1", "CR2"),
  rbind(conventional_att(fit_state), conventional_att(fit_state_cr2))))
```

A cluster that contains a whole cohort has a share of one. The part of its
score from that cohort is zero under CR2, where its factor is zero, and, on a
balanced panel, under CR1, where the cohort's centered residuals cancel. That
cohort's sampling variation is then omitted. In these data, the 2004 cohort
(adoption index 4 in the tables) lies in a single state with no other counties, and that state's score is zero
under both covariances. For every other cluster, the CR2 adjustment grows with
its share.

### A small panel for procedural examples

The next data are artificial: 72 units observed in four periods, of which 24 are
never treated, 24 adopt in period 3, and 24 adopt in period 4. The last cohort
has one post-treatment period and enough pre-treatment history. Later sections
use this inexpensive design to illustrate procedures and options; its results
are not findings.

```{r small-panel}
set.seed(314159)
small <- expand.grid(id = seq_len(72), time = seq_len(4))
small$g <- rep(c(0, 3, 4), each = 24)[small$id]
small$D <- as.integer(small$g > 0 & small$time >= small$g)
small$Y <- 1 + small$id / 100 + .06 * small$time + .08 * small$D +
  rnorm(nrow(small), sd = .08)
small_fit <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = small, index = c("id", "time"), estimator = "imp")
tab(small_fit$diagnostics$cohort_counts)
```

### Missing observations and treatment dating

Outcomes are never imputed. After a known treatment status, a missing status or
an absent row is filled forward within unit; an unknown leading status stays
unknown, and its outcome is excluded. Adoption is dated at the first observed
treated status, so a missing stretch around adoption can hide the true date.

```{r missing-panel}
incomplete <- small[!(small$id == 1 & small$time == 2), ]
incomplete$Y[incomplete$id == 2 & incomplete$time == 3] <- NA
incomplete$D[incomplete$id == 25 & incomplete$time == 2] <- NA
incomplete$D[incomplete$id == 26 & incomplete$time == 1] <- NA
incomplete$D[incomplete$id == 27 & incomplete$time == 3] <- NA
incomplete_fit <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = incomplete, index = c("id", "time"),
                             estimator = "cs_nt")
missing_counts <- unlist(incomplete_fit$data_info$missingness)
tab(data.frame(diagnostic = names(missing_counts), value = unname(missing_counts)))
history <- incomplete_fit$data_info$panel
tab(history[history$unit_id %in% c("1", "2", "25", "26", "27"),
  c("unit_id", "calendar_time", "Y", "D_original", "D", "observed_row",
    "treatment_filled", "usable", "cohort")])
```

The fit warns that the design is unbalanced. Estimation uses the observed
histories, while `W` uses fixed cohort masses and the balanced mapping, so the
paper's balanced-panel coverage and equivalence results do not automatically
apply. Check `cell_counts` before interpreting estimates: every required
comparison must be estimable, and every included unit must have at least one
usable outcome.

```{r irregular-labels}
irregular <- small
irregular$time <- c(2001, 2002, 2004, 2007)[irregular$time]
irregular_fit <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = irregular, index = c("id", "time"),
                            estimator = "cs_nt")
tab(data.frame(analysis_index = seq_along(irregular_fit$data_info$time_labels),
  calendar_label = irregular_fit$data_info$time_labels))
```

Irregular numeric or date labels draw a warning and are treated as equally
spaced analysis periods; character labels are used in sorted order. Treatment
must be binary and absorbing, with a never-treated group and an observed
untreated period for each treated unit. Units already treated at their first
known status are not supported.

## 3. Targets and representations in the application {#targets}

A target averages selected post-treatment cells. For selected cells \(J\), a
cell in cohort \(g\) receives weight \(\ell_j=m_g/\sum_{k\in J}m_{g(k)}\),
where \(m_g\) is the cohort mass. The ATT selects all post-treatment cells, and
earlier cohorts contribute more of them. A dynamic target selects one relative
period, and a cohort-dynamic target selects one cell.

```{r empirical-sensitivity}
M_application <- c(0, .005, .01, .015, .02)
att <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                          target = "att", seed = 123)
dynamic <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = .015,
                              target = "dynamic", seed = 123)
cohort_dynamic <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = .015,
                                     target = "cohort-dynamic", seed = 123)
att_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                                    target = "att", framework = "aggregate", seed = 123)
dynamic_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = .015,
                                        target = "dynamic", framework = "aggregate",
                                        seed = 123)
tab(rows(list(cohort_ATT = att, aggregate_ATT = att_aggregate)))
```

SD bounds the second differences of each cohort's block-bias path,
\(|\Delta_{g,s}-2\Delta_{g,s-1}+\Delta_{g,s-2}|\leq M\), here in
log-employment units. These calls use the defaults (C-LF, post-only). A
larger `M` permits more curvature; the conventional estimate does not depend
on `M`.

```{r empirical-att-plots, fig.height=4.5}
plot(att, main = "Cohort restrictions: minimum-wage ATT", ylab = "Log teen employment")
plot(att_aggregate, main = "Aggregate restrictions: minimum-wage ATT",
     ylab = "Log teen employment")
```

The dotted line is the conventional estimate, and the shaded band, drawn when
its bounds are finite, is the plug-in identified set. Under the post-only
restriction, the plug-in set is never empty, because the pre-treatment path is
not restricted. The full-path restriction also bounds the curvature of the
estimated pre-treatment paths. In this application those paths violate it at
every displayed `M`, and the full-path plug-in sets are empty. The next chunk
computes the full-path FLCI for comparison.

```{r empirical-plugin-status}
att_flci <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                               target = "att", method = "FLCI", seed = 123)
tab(data.frame(M = M_application,
  post_only_plugin_empty = vapply(att$results,
    function(z) isTRUE(z$diagnostics$plugin.empty), logical(1)),
  full_path_plugin_empty = vapply(att_flci$results,
    function(z) isTRUE(z$diagnostics$plugin.empty), logical(1))))
tab(rows(list(post_only_CLF = att, full_path_FLCI = att_flci)))
```

The plug-in calculation treats the estimated paths as fixed, whereas the FLCI
accounts for sampling uncertainty and can be nonempty when the plug-in set is
empty. An empty full-path plug-in set is therefore not by itself a
specification test. The FLCI's optimized center can differ from the
conventional estimate.

Aggregate inference transforms the estimates and covariance to \(A\hat\beta\)
and \(A\Sigma A'\) and restricts the aggregated coefficients. The same
numerical `M` therefore imposes a different assumption under cohort and
aggregate inference.

On a balanced panel, appropriately normalized Imp and CS-NYT block biases
differ only by cohort constants, which the SD and RM restrictions do not
detect, so their cohort identified sets coincide. Because the package uses a
common covariance construction and FLCI selection rule, the theoretical
confidence sets coincide as well, under CR1 or CR2 (the CR2 shares do not
depend on the estimator). Computed sets agree up to numerical precision when
controls and seeds match, although either search can report an unresolved
result. The equivalence does not cover conventional coefficients and standard
errors, CS-NT, aggregate restrictions, covariances supplied to
`cohort_input()`, or unbalanced panels. The comparison below uses the same
bounds, seed, covariance, representation, and procedure.

```{r balanced-cohort-comparison}
att_nyt <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_nyt, restriction = "SD", M = M_application,
                              target = "att", seed = 123)
tab(data.frame(M = att$intervals$M, Imp_status = att$intervals$status,
  CS_NYT_status = att_nyt$intervals$status,
  lower_difference = att$intervals$lower - att_nyt$intervals$lower,
  upper_difference = att$intervals$upper - att_nyt$intervals$upper), digits = 10)
```

```{r target-weights}
target_weights <- function(x) do.call(rbind, lapply(x$targets, function(z) {
  j <- which(z$target != 0)
  data.frame(target = z$id, coordinate = names(z$target)[j],
             weight = as.numeric(z$target[j]))
}))
tab(target_weights(att))
tab(target_weights(dynamic))
tab(rows(list(cohort_framework = dynamic, aggregate_framework = dynamic_aggregate)))
```

The weights show which cells define each estimand. Dynamic targets at
different periods can average different cohorts, so changes across periods
need not reflect a fixed cohort mix.

```{r empirical-dynamic-plots, fig.height=5.2}
plot(dynamic, M = .015, main = "Dynamic effects at M = .015",
     ylab = "Log teen employment")
chosen_cohort <- sort(unique(fit_imp$coordinate_info$cohort))[1]
plot(cohort_dynamic, M = .015, cohorts = chosen_cohort,
     main = "One cohort: conventional estimates and sensitivity sets",
     ylab = "Log teen employment")
```

In `plot()`, `M` selects bounds that were already computed, and `cohorts`
selects cohorts by adoption index; neither reruns inference.

### Balanced targets and balanced aggregation {#balanced}

The balanced window contains the relative periods observed for every cohort.
In this application it runs from \(s=-2\), the first period of the 2004
cohort, to \(s=1\), because the 2007 cohort is treated for one year. With
`balanced = TRUE` the ATT averages the window's post-treatment cells with the
same cohort weights in every period, here the effect in the first treated year.
Aggregate inference then forms the aggregated event study only on the window,
so the same cohorts enter every period.

```{r balanced-targets}
M_balanced <- c(0, .01, .02)
att_balanced <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, M = M_balanced, balanced = TRUE, seed = 123)
att_balanced_window <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, M = M_balanced, balanced = TRUE,
                                          cohort.paths = "window", seed = 123)
att_balanced_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(fit_imp, M = M_balanced, balanced = TRUE,
                                             framework = "aggregate", seed = 123)
att_balanced$settings$window
tab(target_weights(att_balanced))
tab(rows(list(cohort_full = att_balanced, cohort_window = att_balanced_window,
              aggregate = att_balanced_aggregate)))
print(att_balanced_aggregate)
```

Under cohort inference, `cohort.paths = "full"`, the default, keeps each
cohort's whole path, as in the paper. `cohort.paths = "window"` uses each path
only inside the window: the RM benchmark comes from the pre-treatment changes
in the window, the full-path SD restriction bounds only the pre-treatment
second differences in the window, and later periods are dropped. Under the
post-only SD restriction used here, the two choices give the same plug-in
identified set, and their confidence sets differ at most slightly. With one
post-treatment period in the window, the post-only plug-in identified set is
also the same under aggregate inference; the confidence sets differ because
the two analyses use different coefficients and covariances.

Balanced aggregation changes the estimand. It removes the change in the
cohorts averaged across periods, but not the change in the not-yet-treated
comparison groups, which enters the imputation and CS-NYT biases through the
bias map. In the paper's simulations, aggregate inference on the balanced
window comes closer to cohort inference but still differs from it. On a
balanced panel, Imp and CS-NYT give the same balanced cohort inference under
either `cohort.paths` value, but in general not the same aggregate inference.
Balanced aggregate results store the aggregation matrix, the aggregated
coefficients, and their covariance in `aggregation`.

## 4. Procedures and SD scopes {#procedures}

The six comparisons below cross the three procedures with the two SD scopes.
More pre-treatment periods give the full-path restriction more information
about curvature. The comparisons use the artificial panel with 200 calibration
draws and a 21-point grid to keep the guide quick. These are demonstration settings,
not the defaults or a recommendation.

```{r six-method-scope-cases}
illustrative_control <- list(lf.sims = 200L, grid.points = 21L)
sd_examples <- list()
for (method in c("FLCI", "Conditional", "C-LF")) {
  for (full in c(FALSE, TRUE)) {
    label <- paste(method, if (full) "full path" else "post-only")
    sd_examples[[label]] <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "SD",
      M = c(0, .015), method = method, full.path = full, target = "att",
      seed = 2026, control = illustrative_control)
  }
}
tab(rows(sd_examples))
```

The FLCI optimizes a linear estimator, accounting for its standard deviation
and worst-case bias. C-LF adds a least-favorable first stage, calibrated by
simulation, to the conditional test. The procedures need not give the same set
or center; the table lists each piece of a set on its own row.

```{r default-dispatch}
default_sd <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, M = .015, seed = 2026)
flci_sd <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, M = .015, method = "FLCI", seed = 2026)
tab(rows(list(default_SD = default_sd, FLCI_SD = flci_sd)))
```

With `method = NULL`, the package uses C-LF for both SD and RM. For SD,
`full.path = NULL` means `FALSE` for C-LF and Conditional and `TRUE` for the
FLCI, so `method = "FLCI"` alone requests the full-path FLCI. The FLCI uses
the pure pre-treatment second differences only under the full-path
restriction, in addition to the last two pre-treatment periods that every
post-only procedure extrapolates. Its coverage guarantee then no longer holds
when those second differences exceed `M`, and its coverage also deteriorates
when some cohorts contain only a few units.

## 5. Relative-magnitude restrictions {#rm}

RM bounds each post-treatment change in a cohort's block bias,
\(|\Delta_{g,s}-\Delta_{g,s-1}|\), by \(\bar M\) times the same cohort's largest
absolute pre-treatment change; the bound has no units. The paper recommends
choosing between RM and SD based on the empirical context. The cohort
restriction is a union of cases, one for each combination of where and with
which sign each cohort's largest pre-treatment change occurs. In the
minimum-wage application each positive bound requires 320 cases, and the
examples therefore use the artificial panel.

With `framework = "aggregate"`, RM restricts the aggregated coefficients using
the aggregated path's own pre-treatment benchmark, not a separate benchmark
for each cohort.

```{r rm-procedures}
rm_clf <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "RM", M = c(0, 1),
                             method = "C-LF", seed = 2026, control = illustrative_control)
rm_conditional <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "RM", M = c(0, 1),
                                     method = "Conditional", seed = 2026,
                                     control = illustrative_control)
rm_aggregate <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, restriction = "RM", M = c(0, 1),
                                   framework = "aggregate", seed = 2026,
                                   control = illustrative_control)
tab(rows(list(cohort_CLF = rm_clf, cohort_Conditional = rm_conditional,
              aggregate_CLF = rm_aggregate)))
plot(rm_clf, main = "Artificial panel: RM confidence sets", ylab = "Artificial effect")
```

RM has no full-path option and no FLCI; requesting either is an input error.

## 6. Read and reuse results {#results}

A `cohort_fit` holds the coefficients `betahat`, their full covariance `Sigma`,
the bias map `W`, the `normalization`, the coefficient labels
`coordinate_info`, the cohort masses, and sample diagnostics; `coef()` and
`vcov()` extract the first two. A sensitivity result holds the conventional
target estimates, every piece of each confidence set, the settings, and
per-task diagnostics, including, for Conditional inference, the searched
ranges that `summary()` tabulates.

```{r print-and-summary}
print(default_sd)
print(summary(default_sd))
```

### Extracting confidence sets

```{r extract-results}
conditional <- sd_examples[["Conditional full path"]]
tab(conditional$estimates)
tab(sets(conditional))
tab(conditional$results[[1]]$components)
```

Each target and bound can occupy several rows of `intervals`, one for each
piece. Keep the `component` column and every row when saving results; taking
`min(lower)` and `max(upper)` would fill the gaps between pieces.
`results[[k]]` follows the target order, then the sorted bounds.

```{r flci-details}
f <- flci_sd$results[[1]]
tab(data.frame(conventional_estimate = flci_sd$estimates$estimate,
  optimized_center = mean(c(f$components$lower, f$components$upper)),
  standard_error = f$diagnostics$standard.error,
  maximum_bias = f$diagnostics$maximum.bias,
  half_length = f$diagnostics$half.length,
  solver_status = f$diagnostics$solver.status))
```

The FLCI's linear weights (`results[[k]]$weights`) determine its optimized
center, and the trade-off between its standard deviation and worst-case bias
determines its half-length.

### Outcomes and statuses

Each target and bound ends in one of these outcomes:

| Outcome | Meaning | How to recognize it |
|---|---|---|
| Nonempty set | One or more computed pieces | `success = TRUE`; bounds may be infinite |
| Certified empty set | C-LF's least-favorable first stage rejects every value | `success = TRUE`, status `empty`, missing bounds |
| Unresolved empty search | A finite search accepted no value and no certificate applies | `success = FALSE`, status `uncertified_empty_search`, warning |
| Unsupported task | No sampling variation in the target or tested moments, or too little pre-treatment history | `success = FALSE`, a status such as `unsupported_zero_variance` or `insufficient_prehistory`, warning |
| Numerical failure or limit | The search or solver failed or did not finish within its controls | `success = FALSE`, a status such as `evaluation_limit` or `inference_error`, message, warning |
| Invalid input | An argument or data requirement is violated | Error; no inference is run |

Read each row's `status` and `message` rather than relying on a fixed list of
status names. Further details are in these places:

| Where | What to check |
|---|---|
| `result$intervals` | Every piece of each set, with bounds, center, plug-in bounds, `success`, `status`, and `message` |
| `result$estimates`, `result$targets` | Conventional estimates and the cell weights that define each target |
| `result$results[[k]]` | Detailed output for one target and bound, including procedure diagnostics and FLCI weights |
| `result$settings` | The options used and the assigned task seeds |
| `result$aggregation` | With `balanced = TRUE` under aggregate inference: the aggregation matrix, aggregated coefficients, covariance, and normalization on the balanced window |
| `summary(result)$search.ranges` | The ranges a Conditional search covered |
| `fit$diagnostics` | Cohort and cell counts, clusters, covariance rank, and `flags` for unbalanced designs, few clusters, single-cluster cells, extra rank loss, or near-zero post-treatment variance |
| `fit$data_info$missingness` | Absent rows, missing outcomes, filled treatment statuses, and outcomes excluded by unknown leading statuses |
| `fit$cluster_shares` | Under CR2, each cluster's share of its cohort and the factor applied to its score |

Before reporting a result, check its status, the sample support, the covariance
diagnostics, and, for Conditional inference, the searched range. Then report
the target and its weights, the cohort or aggregate representation, the
restriction and the units of its bound, the procedure and SD scope, the
confidence level, and every piece of the set.

## 7. Numerical controls and reproducibility {#controls}

All numerical controls go in one uniquely named `control` list.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `lf.sims` | `2000` | C-LF calibration draws (not bootstrap replications) |
| `grid.points` | `101` | Grid points, at least 5; for Conditional searches with `grid.radius` above 8, the reference density |
| `endpoint.tol` | `NULL` | Endpoint tolerance in outcome units; by default 1e-5 times the conventional target standard error |
| `grid.radius` | `8` | Initial search margin for Conditional and RM C-LF (see `?cohort_sensitivity`); not used by SD C-LF |
| `max.expansions` | `6` | Range doublings for Conditional, including the two expansions needed to confirm a stable range (0 or 1 returns no set), and range expansions for RM C-LF; not used by SD C-LF |
| `max.refinements` | `3` | Finer-grid retries after an unresolved search; 0 disables them |
| `max.evaluations` | `100000` | Point evaluations per target and bound, counted across all probes, audits, and retries |
| `topology.audit` | `TRUE` | `FALSE` skips the interior grid comparisons; domain and endpoint checks remain |
| `max.components` | `100000` | Maximum number of RM cases |
| `flci.solver` | `"direct"` | FLCI optimizer, `"direct"` or `"nested"` (requires CVXR) |
| `flci.control` | `list()` | Solver-specific settings, listed below |

More calibration draws reduce the Monte Carlo noise in C-LF, and a denser grid
adds point tests; both take more time. For final results, increase the
calibration draws and check the numerical diagnostics.

Conditional and C-LF sets come from a finite numerical search. A Conditional
search does not rule out pieces outside the range it searched, which
`summary(result)$search.ranges` reports. For SD, C-LF searches a range that its
first stage certifies (if it cannot certify one, it reports no set), but this
certifies only the outer range, not the interior. Any finite grid can miss
very narrow pieces or gaps. The evaluation count does not limit running time.

```{r search-limits}
limited <- cohort_sensitivity(small_fit, M = .015, method = "Conditional", seed = 2026,
  control = list(grid.points = 21L, max.evaluations = 10L))
tab(limited$intervals[, c("status", "message")])
```

The warning and failed status mark a computational limit: the calculation
stopped before it resolved the set, so the result is neither an empty
confidence set nor a rejection.

With an explicit `seed`, each task receives a fixed random-number stream, the
results do not depend on the number of workers, and the caller's random-number
state is restored; `seed = NULL` draws the task seeds from the caller's stream.
`parallel = TRUE` runs independent target and bound tasks, or the cases of a
single RM task, on `cores` workers.

### FLCI solvers {#solvers}

| Solver | `flci.control` key | Default and constraint |
|---|---|---|
| direct | `n_random_starts` | `8L`, nonnegative integer |
| direct | `maxit` | `20000L`, nonnegative integer |
| nested | `solver` | `"ECOS"`, one available CVXR solver name |
| nested | `solver_opts` | `list()`, named options passed to CVXR |
| nested | `outer_tol` | `1e-7`, positive |
| nested | `grid_size` | `15L`, integer at least 3 |
| nested | `feasibility_tol` | `1e-6`, positive |
| nested | `objective_tol` | `1e-6`, positive |

Each key belongs to its solver, and the two lists cannot be mixed.

## 8. Supply external estimates and construct W {#external}

External input needs the full named vector of cohort-period coefficients
\(\hat\beta\) (pre-treatment, reference, and post-treatment), its joint
covariance \(\Sigma\), an invertible bias map \(W\) with \(\delta=W\Delta\), and
deterministic normalization constraints \(N\) with \(N\hat\beta=0\) and
\(N\Sigma=0\); \(W\) must preserve the normalization. The covariance may be
singular (positive semidefinite), as normalizations usually make it. The
pre-treatment coefficients must be block-bias estimates as defined in the
paper. Marginal standard errors, an aggregated event study, or residual
pre-trends do not carry this information.

The round trip below passes the artificial fit's estimates through
`cohort_input()` and reruns the default analysis.

```{r external-roundtrip}
external <- cohort_input(betahat = coef(small_fit), vcov = vcov(small_fit),
  coefficient_info = small_fit$coordinate_info, W = small_fit$W,
  normalization = small_fit$normalization,
  cohort_sizes = small_fit$cohort_masses, estimator = "imp")
external_result <- cohort_sensitivity(external, M = .015, seed = 2026)
tab(rows(list(internal = default_sd, external = external_result)))
```

`coefficient_info` needs the columns `coordinate`, integer `cohort`, integer
`relative_period`, and `type` (`"pre"` for pre-treatment and reference
coefficients, `"post"` otherwise). `betahat` must be named; the covariance and
`W` need row and column names, and the normalization needs column names, that
match the coefficient labels, and `cohort_input()` aligns them. `cohort_sizes`
needs one positive finite value per treated cohort, named by its adoption
index.

### W describes a mapping, not an estimator

```{r mappings}
W_nyt <- build_W(cohort_times = c(3, 4), cohort_sizes = c(`3` = 24, `4` = 24),
                 never_treated_size = 24, n_periods = 4, estimator = "cs_nyt")
dim(W_nyt)
W_nyt[grepl("delta_post", rownames(W_nyt)), , drop = FALSE]
```

`build_W()` constructs the bias map for a balanced design with fixed cohort
sizes; it does not estimate coefficients or covariances. `cohort_times` are
distinct integer adoption indices from 2 to `n_periods`, and all sizes,
including the never-treated size, must be positive.

### Too little pre-treatment history

A fit can have too little pre-treatment history for sensitivity analysis:

```{r short-history}
short_history <- cohort_fit(Y ~ D, data = subset(small, time >= 2),
                            index = c("id", "time"), estimator = "cs_nt")
short_result <- cohort_sensitivity(short_history, M = .015, seed = 2026)
tab(sets(short_result))
tab(short_result$intervals[, c("status", "message")])
```

Under cohort inference, every treated cohort needs at least two pre-treatment
periods; this task returns `insufficient_prehistory` and no set. One
post-treatment period is enough, as for the period-4 cohort of the full
artificial panel.

## 9. Plot choices {#plots}

Fit plots accept `type = "dynamic"` (the default) or `"cohort-dynamic"`;
sensitivity plots take their form from the computed target. `main`, `xlab`,
and `ylab` set the labels, and `color` overrides the framework color. All plots
return ggplot objects, which accept further ggplot2 layers.

```{r plot-options, fig.height=5.2}
plot(fit_imp, type = "cohort-dynamic", cohorts = chosen_cohort,
  main = "Conventional coefficients for one cohort",
  xlab = "Relative period", ylab = "Log teen employment")
plot(att, M = c(0, .015, .02), identified.set = FALSE,
  main = "Selected minimum-wage bounds",
  xlab = "Allowed curvature M", ylab = "Log teen employment", color = "#5A3E85") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

`identified.set = FALSE` removes the plug-in band from ATT plots without
changing the confidence sets. `paper_palette()` returns the package's colors for
representations, procedures, or cohorts.
